corrections.source_says: Set criterion_3_outcome_scored_on_output to met and revise the associated reason. The paper states that major deliverables were graded with analytic rubrics; Figure 6 explicitly connects individual deliverables produced to scoring by a single rater using the same rubric for both cohorts, and Section 3.2 identifies Creativity thinking as a rubric dimension. This supports an instructor rating of produced work, consistent with S1-O1.scored_on_output=true. The absence of detailed scoring anchors is a measurement limitation, not evidence that only self-reports were collected. Core eligibility remains no because assignment was nonrandom and fewer than 50 people were analyzed.

corrections.source_says: Complete the reporting of the graded design-work rubric with Problem solving and Presentation, retaining their exact labels and using construct=other rather than inferring a more specific creativity construct. Problem solving: historical 78.58 (SD 5.85), intervention 84.94 (SD 4.30), difference 6.36, bootstrap 95% CI [2.40, 10.00], Welch p = 0.005, Hedges’ g = 1.23, Mann-Whitney p = 0.007. Presentation: historical 79.25 (SD 5.05), intervention 82.69 (SD 5.56), difference 3.44, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.29, 7.17], Welch p = 0.100, Hedges’ g = 0.62, Mann-Whitney p = 0.069. These are results for the same historical and intervention students, not additional people or studies.

confirmed: The source is the full 31-page arXiv:2609.18505v1 [cs.HC], dated 16 Sep 2026; the title and authors Hong Qu, Zichao Ling, and Yadie Yang match the form (p. 1 and PDF page count). The entire markdown, including references and Appendix A, was read.

One nonrandomized historical-cohort study is reported; students were explicitly not randomly assigned. design_class=quasi_people, context_class=observational, criterion_1=not_met, and has_randomized_people_study=false are supported (pp. 9-10, Section 3.1; pp. 19-20, limitations).

The analyzed samples are 12 historical-control students and 16 intervention students, totaling 28 people, not generated images, design artifacts, or ratings. This is below 50; randomized counts appropriately remain null, and no exclusions are stated (p. 9, Section 3.1; pp. 11-13, Sections 3.4-4.1).
Both cohorts were third-year undergraduates with the same instructor, project brief, deliverables, rubric, and grading scheme (p. 9, Section 3.1).

The intervention combines flipped preparation, a platform, gallery exemplars, and GenAI ideation; the comparison cannot isolate a GenAI-only effect. The historical control prepared by previewing slides (pp. 4-11, Sections 1-3.3).

Creativity thinking and Design skills were instructor-rated rubric dimensions on a 0-100 scale, weighted 35% and 20%; the weighted total also includes attendance (p. 10, Section 3.2 and Table 1; p. 11, Section 3.4).

Creativity thinking: historical 79.50 (SD 3.97), intervention 84.38 (SD 4.59), difference 4.88, bootstrap 95% CI [1.81, 8.02], Welch p = 0.006, Hedges’ g = 1.09, Mann-Whitney p = 0.032; n = 12 versus 16. Every number in S1-O1.reported and the one-line finding matches (p. 13, Table 2 and Section 4.1; p. 14, Section 4.1).

Design skills: historical 78.42 (SD 3.40), intervention 84.13 (SD 4.24), difference 5.71, bootstrap 95% CI [2.98, 8.35], Welch p < 0.001, Hedges’ g = 1.42, Mann-Whitney p = 0.001. S1-O2.reported matches (p. 13, Table 2; p. 14, Section 4.1).

Weighted total: historical 80.04 (SD 4.12), intervention 84.91 (SD 3.29), difference 4.87, bootstrap 95% CI [2.16, 7.48], Welch p = 0.003, Hedges’ g = 1.29, Mann-Whitney p = 0.009. S1-O3.reported matches (p. 13, Table 2; p. 14, Section 4.1).

The reported intervals are for raw intervention-minus-historical mean differences, not for Hedges’ g. They use percentile bootstrap resampling of individuals within cohorts over 5,000 iterations; analysis is at the individual level (p. 12, Section 3.5; p. 13, Table 2 note).

The commercial image-generation API footnote points to seed.bytedance.com/zh/seedream4_5; students could provide one to three reference images. GenAI supported early visual ideation rather than producing final assessed artifacts (p. 3, Introduction; pp. 7-8, GenAI module, including visual inspection of p. 7 footnote 1).
The course had four lecture sessions followed by nine studio sessions, with the final studio session used for the final presentation (p. 5, Section 2).

The pre/post questionnaires concern the same intervention cohort and use nonidentical self-report items; they are not a separate randomized study or an output-based creativity test. This paper is not a synthesis, so no pooled estimates apply (pp. 11-12, Sections 3.4-3.5; pp. 26-31, Appendix A).
summary: The nonrandomized comparison analyzed 12 historical-control and 16 intervention students, and all existing reported statistics and the arXiv v1 identification match the PDF. The form needs its included appendix recorded, criterion 3 marked met, and the omitted problem-solving and presentation rubric results added; no randomized people study is present.
